extracted.intended_audience: researchers, students, faculty, and librarians interested in comics/graphic-novels archival materials
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what the Columbia Rare Book & Manuscript Library (RBML) collects and preserves for comics/graphic-novels research, including emphases, acceptable material types, and example collection contents. Useful for donors, researchers, and archivists assessing relevance and access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting emphasis / scope
rubrics_metrics.description: RBML collects archives of comics creators, editors, and publishers, with an emphasis on New York-area professionals and materials that document the history of comics publishing, in keeping with RBML’s larger focus on the history of publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statement defines the primary topical/geographic scope for acquisitions and accessioning: priority to creators/editors/publishers (particularly New York–area) and to materials that document publishing history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of fan culture materials
rubrics_metrics.description: RBML also collects materials related to comics fan culture, especially convention material, fanzines, and fan mail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fan-produced and fan-related items are explicitly considered collecting material and support research/teaching in comics studies as an interdisciplinary field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepted materials / formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials of interest include manuscripts, drafts, original art, roughs and tracings, correspondence, contracts, records, fanzines, artifacts, and other formats in support of research and teaching in comics studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list of formats establishes the kinds of physical and documentary materials RBML expects to acquire — creative files, business/legal records, process materials, and ephemera are all within scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creator-archive content expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Creator archives commonly include sketches, sketchbooks, scrapbooks, tearsheets, photographs, printed material, original artwork, drafts, manuscripts, scripts, project proposals, story ideas, business records, fan mail, and correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from named collections (Charles Saxon, Chris Claremont, Wendy and Richard Pini, Jerry Robinson, Al Jaffee, Howard Cruse, etc.) indicate typical item types and that creator archives may document creative process, professional career, and fan/public engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher/press archive content
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher archives (e.g., Kitchen Sink Press) may include large runs of correspondence from cartoonists, business records, mechanicals, and other publishing files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher holdings document editorial/publishing practices and contain abundant business- and production-related materials useful for the history of comics publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching collection / pedagogical purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic Art Collection is a teaching collection of original comic art intended to shed light on various historical styles or techniques and includes newspaper strip art, comic book art, comic books, and ephemera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material selected for instructional use should illustrate styles, techniques, and historical contexts, not just be representative holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community/regional collecting (New York comics community)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cumulative New York comics community collection of original art and process materials creates a snapshot of the work of the comics community in the NYC metropolitan area and allows researchers to track who was working here, when, and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes a collecting principle to build geographically-focused, cumulative documentation of a creative community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special-topic collections / award-related materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Collections related to awards or festivals (e.g., MoCCA Arts Fest Awards, Pulitzer Prizes collection) include winners' exhibits and may be accompanied by entry forms, letters of support, photographs of winners, biographies, original art, tearsheets, and photostats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award- and festival-related holdings document institutional recognition and can include administrative documentation useful for provenance and research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological and scope breadth of holdings
rubrics_metrics.description: Collections cover wide chronological ranges (examples: Dennis Ryan editorial cartoon art dating back to the 1880s; S. Clay Wilson material dating from early childhood to later career), indicating collections may span decades and multiple career phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donors and researchers should expect holdings of varying temporal breadth; long chronological coverage is within RBML practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of legal and business records
rubrics_metrics.description: Archives may contain legal files, contracts, business records, and litigation-related materials (e.g., Mark Tye papers include legal files related to litigation; many creator collections include business records and contracts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The collecting scope explicitly includes documentation of legal/business aspects of creators' careers, which is relevant for rights, provenance, and scholarly research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access and processing status notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some collections are described as 'unprocessed but accessible' or 'not yet processed for use,' indicating that a collection's processing status does not necessarily make it unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should check access conditions; unprocessed status may affect discoverability and handling but items can still be made accessible on request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquisition sources and donation provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Collections and holdings often derive from donations by creators, alumni, collectors, and institutions (examples: Jonathan Zeitlin collection donated by an alumnus; Kitchen Sink Press archives from the publisher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provenance via donation is a common acquisition route; descriptions may note the donor and circumstances, which inform access and rights considerations.
